extra_misconceptions.fact: Qualified Supervision under Safe Swim Defense requires a mature, conscientious adult who is at least twenty-one years of age.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A certified lifeguard on duty satisfies the Qualified Supervision requirement even if that lifeguard is only eighteen years old.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Safe Swim Defense limits the maximum water depth in the designated swimmer zone to twelve feet in clear water to allow bottom recovery.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The swimmer ability zone in a natural lake may extend to any bottom depth once all swimmers pass the hundred-yard classification test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Audible buddy checks must occur roughly every ten minutes so supervisors can verify every pair is together inside their assigned zone.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Buddy checks are only necessary at the start and end of a troop swim session when a dedicated lookout watches the water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The lookout must remain free of rescue duties to scan the entire swim area continuously while separate response personnel stand ready.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: One person standing on a dock can fulfill both the lookout and response personnel duties at the same time for a small troop.

extra_socratic_questions: What steps must the adult supervisor take to inspect and mark a natural lake bottom before opening the three ability zones?
Why is the lookout assigned a separate vantage point from the lifeguards rather than combining both roles into one person?
What maximum water depth and buddy check time interval must be maintained for the nonswimmer and swimmer zones?
Which rescue equipment must be staged with response personnel when setting up a temporary swim area at a wilderness lake?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The four-hundred-yard prerequisite must be swum continuously without resting on walls, lane lines, or the bottom between stroke changes.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A Scout may pause on the pool wall for thirty seconds between each fifty-yard stroke segment during the four-hundred-yard test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Four fifty-yard segments total only two hundred yards, so the swimmer must complete two hundred additional continuous yards to reach 400.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Completing fifty yards of each of the four listed strokes equals the entire distance needed to pass the prerequisite swim test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rhythmic breathing requires exhaling steadily underwater and inhaling quickly to the side so carbon dioxide never builds up in the lungs.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Holding your breath for several strokes during the front crawl builds better endurance than exhaling underwater on every cycle.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Elementary backstroke uses a simultaneous whip kick paired with an underwater arm recovery that stays below the level of the shoulders.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The elementary backstroke uses an alternating flutter kick and overhead arm recovery to maximize forward speed in open water.

extra_socratic_questions: In what order should you sequence the four required strokes during the 400-yard swim to conserve leg power for rescue drills?
What distinguishes the scissor kick used in the sidestroke from the whip kick required during the breaststroke and backstroke?
What distance benchmark must a counselor record for each of the four strokes before approving the continuous 400-yard swim?
Why is it dangerous to attempt deep-water contact rescues if a rescuer cannot glide efficiently with elementary backstroke?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The instinctive drowning response presses the arms laterally against the water and prevents shouting because breathing takes priority.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: An active drowning victim always waves both arms above the water and shouts loudly for help before slipping beneath the surface.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Swimmers caught in a rip current should swim parallel to the shoreline until out of the narrow seaward flow before angling to shore.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Swimming straight back toward the beach with maximum sprint effort is the fastest way to break free from an ocean rip current.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Water rescue follows the Reach, Throw, Row, Go progression so the rescuer avoids direct contact and personal risk whenever possible.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Strong swimmers should jump directly into the water first because swimming to a victim is faster than finding a reaching pole.

extra_misconceptions.fact: River current passes through submerged branches while pinning a swimmer against the trunk with hydraulic force that prevents escape.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Strainer hazards in moving rivers push swimmers safely over the top of fallen trees because surface water flows over the logs.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a swimmer direct their stroke to escape a narrow rip current that is pulling them away from the ocean beach?
Which physical indicators differentiate an active instinctive drowning response from a tired swimmer who is merely distressed?
What surface time window does an active drowning victim typically have before submerging if no flotation device arrives?
Why does the Reach, Throw, Row, Go sequence place entering the water to swim as the final option for a trained rescuer?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rescuers must lie flat or crouch low with a wide base of support so a sudden tug on the pole cannot pull them into the deep water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Standing upright at the edge of a dock gives a rescuer the best leverage when extending a pole to a struggling swimmer nearby.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A rigid pole must be swept gently into contact from the side to avoid striking the victim's head or knocking them beneath the water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Thrusting a rigid shepherd's crook or paddle directly at a victim's face helps them see and grab the rescue aid more quickly.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rescuers must brace against the deck wall, keep their weight back, and draw the victim in hand-over-hand without leaning over the edge.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Locking your elbows and leaning forward over the coping speeds up a hand-to-wrist reaching assist at the edge of a deep pool.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A leg-reach assist requires the rescuer to grasp a dock piling, ladder, or shoreline anchor firmly with one hand before extending a foot.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A wading rescuer extending a leg to a victim in chest-deep water can stand freely without holding onto any stationary support.

extra_socratic_questions: Where on the victim's body should you place the tip of a reaching pole so a panicked swimmer does not miss the extension?
Under what condition does a rescuer choose a leg extension in shallow water instead of reaching out with a bare arm from a dock?
What stance and center-of-gravity position keep a rescuer anchored on a wet pool deck while pulling a heavy swimmer to safety?
Why is it dangerous to reach directly with your bare hand when a towel, shirt, or canoe paddle is available within arm's reach?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A ring buoy must be thrown past the victim and slightly upwind or upcurrent so the line settles across their shoulder without injury.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Aiming a heavy ring buoy directly at the victim's head ensures the flotation device lands close enough for an immediate grasp.

extra_misconceptions.fact: For a rapid second throw, the rescuer scoops a small amount of water into the empty bag for weight and throws the coiled line and bag.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A rescue throw bag must be completely repacked with rope before the rescuer can attempt a missed second throw to a swimmer.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Securing the line by stepping on the bitter end or holding it in the non-throwing hand allows instant release if current pulls hard.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tying the bitter end of a throw rope securely around your wrist prevents losing the rescue bag during an energetic underhand toss.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Sudden jerks rip the buoy out of tired hands, so the rescuer must lean back and pull smoothly while watching the victim's grip.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Jerking the retrieval line rapidly pulls a victim on a ring buoy to shore faster than a steady, low-posture hand-over-hand pull.

extra_socratic_questions: Where relative to the victim and current should a tethered ring buoy land so you can draw the floating line into their hands?
What differentiates repacking a rescue throw bag for a second toss from coiling a loose fifty-foot heaving line on a dock?
What minimum throwing distance must you achieve to place a buoyant aid within reach of the practice victim for this requirement?
Why is it dangerous to tie the bitter end of a throw line around your wrist or waist before casting a ring buoy into current?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Loading over a canoe's side gunwale without a counterbalance easily capsizes the craft, so swimmers board over the ends or tow to shore.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pulling an exhausted swimmer directly over the middle gunwale of an empty solo canoe is the safest way to bring them aboard.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A rowboat rescuer pivots near the swimmer and backs the wider, more stable transom within reach so the bow cannot strike the victim.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rowers should drive the bow of a rowboat straight into a struggling victim at full speed to minimize the time spent in open water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every watercraft rescuer must wear a properly fastened life jacket before launching because a panicked swimmer can capsize the boat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A rescuer inside a watercraft does not need to wear a life jacket as long as an extra personal flotation device is thrown out.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Swimmers should hold the bow toggle or stern grab loop of a kayak so they cannot roll the narrow hull by pulling on the high cockpit.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A kayak rescuer should instruct a panicked swimmer to grab the cockpit coaming or the paddler's arms for support in rough water.

extra_socratic_questions: What mechanical advantage does flipping a stand-up paddleboard beside a victim create when loading an exhausted swimmer aboard?
Why should a rowboat approach a conscious swimmer stern-first while a canoe or kayak typically makes contact near the bow or T-bar?
Which wind and surface current observations determine whether a watercraft approaches the swimmer from upwind or downwind?
Where must a rescuer position their weight inside a canoe when a swimmer holds the gunwale so the hull does not capsize?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Buoyant aids support the combined weight of victim and rescuer at the surface, whereas non-buoyant cloth offers zero upward flotation.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A non-buoyant towel or wet shirt works just as well as a rescue tube during a deep-water swimming rescue of a tired adult.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Wearing the shoulder strap lets the rescuer swim with both arms free while the rescue tube trails behind with minimal water drag.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Holding a rescue tube in one hand while swimming the approach stroke is faster than wearing the shoulder strap and towing it.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Improvised buoyant items such as life jackets, air mattresses, sealed water jugs, kickboards, and coolers provide effective flotation.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Only commercially manufactured lifeguard tubes and ring buoys may be used as buoyant aids during an emergency water rescue.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A life jacket used as a presented rescue aid should be towed or pushed ahead rather than worn loosely and removed near a victim.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: An unfastened life jacket worn loosely by the rescuer can be slipped off easily in deep water to hand to a panicked swimmer.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a rescue tube strap sit on your torso while swimming an approach stroke toward a distressed person in open water?
What makes a flexible foam rescue tube safer for close-quarters contact than a hard plastic rescue can in calm swimming areas?
What buoyancy rating or flotation capacity allows an improvised camp item like a sealed cooler or dry bag to support an adult?
Why are buoyant rescue aids preferred over non-buoyant extensions like a shirt or towel when performing a swimming go rescue?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A stride jump or compact jump keeps the rescuer's head above water to maintain visual contact with the victim and avoid bottom impact.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Diving headfirst from a high pier is the safest entry for a swimming rescue because it gets the rescuer past the dock quickly.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rescuers must stop six to ten feet away in a defensive position and push the buoyant aid forward so the victim grabs the float first.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Swimming all the way into arm's reach before stopping allows the rescuer to place the buoyant aid directly under the victim's arms.

extra_misconceptions.fact: An approach stroke must be swum heads-up so the rescuer never loses sight of the victim's exact location if the swimmer submerges.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Putting your face in the water for standard rotary breathing during the approach stroke is best because speed matters most.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Continuous calm instructions and encouragement reassure a conscious victim, gauge their mental state, and encourage cooperative kicking.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Silent concentration during a thirty-foot rescue tow is better than talking because speaking wastes the rescuer's oxygen.

extra_socratic_questions: What body posture and leg action prevent your head from submerging during a stride jump entry into clear, deep open water?
Why must you keep your eyes elevated above the surface during a heads-up front crawl or breaststroke approach to a swimmer?
At what stopping distance from the conscious victim should you transition into a reverse and ready position to present the aid?
What verbal instructions and encouragement should you give while pushing a rescue tube across the final few feet to a victim?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Shoes and pants must come off first so your arms and vision never get trapped inside a wet shirt if you must jump in early.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Removing your shirt first during a timed clothing strip is faster than starting with your shoes and pants.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A wet shirt acts only as a flexible tether to keep you beyond arm's reach while the subject kicks and you pull steadily.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A soaked cotton shirt provides enough trapped air to float a tired swimmer during a 30-foot nonbuoyant tow.

extra_misconceptions.fact: If a victim is submerging immediately or the water is frigid, kicking off only heavy boots and bulky coats saves vital seconds.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rescuers should always strip off every layer of clothing regardless of water temperature or how fast the victim is sinking.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Coiling fabric around your hand or wrist prevents an instant release if the panicked swimmer lunges forward along the cloth.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wrapping the sleeve of a towing shirt tightly around your wrist gives a stronger grip during a deep-water pull.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to pull a pullover shirt over your head before untying and kicking off heavy shoes on shore?
Under what condition does a rescuer leave light street clothes on rather than taking 20 seconds to strip on shore?
What distance from a conscious subject confirms you stopped outside their lunging reach before extending a wet shirt?
What happens to the rescuer if the panicked subject pulls hard on the shirt and the rescuer fails to let go immediately?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Panicked victims at the surface often cannot process speech and will reflexively climb onto anything within arm's reach.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Calm verbal reassurance alone will convince a panicked person in the instinctive drowning response to stop thrashing.

extra_misconceptions.fact: You must pace yourself just six to ten feet ahead, facing the swimmer with breaststroke or backstroke while coaching them.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Lead-and-wait requires swimming far ahead of the distressed subject so you can reach the dock first to get help.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The reverse-and-ready posture keeps your legs extended forward toward the victim so you can kick backward immediately.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stopping upright with your feet straight down is the fastest posture for backing away from a lunging swimmer.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Adrenaline gives a drowning person enough leverage in weightless water to push even a much heavier rescuer underwater.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Larger, stronger lifeguards can safely grab an active drowning adult from the front without risking submersion.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a Scout position the hips and legs during a reverse-and-ready stop just outside an active victim's reach?
Which physical indicator separates a panicked active drowning subject from a tired swimmer who can follow voice coaching?
What minimum buffer distance keeps you safe from a sudden lunge while coaching a distressed swimmer toward shallow water?
Why is it dangerous to swim directly into a thrashing subject's arms instead of waiting for exhaustion or submersion?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The cross-chest carry is exhausting and restrictive, so calm tired swimmers should be moved with a lighter wrist or armpit tow.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A cross-chest carry is always the best first choice for any conscious swimmer because it gives maximum control.

extra_misconceptions.fact: You grasp one wrist with your opposite hand and swim sidestroke while the subject floats on their back with their free arm.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: During a wrist tow, the rescuer swims breaststroke while pulling both of the tired swimmer's wrists behind them.

extra_misconceptions.fact: You must swim behind the subject, place a hand under their upper arm to level them, and keep yourself clear of sudden grabs.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Approaching from the front for an armpit tow lets you lock hands faster with a cooperative swimmer in deep water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Continuous calm talking keeps a frightened swimmer relaxed, reminds them to float high, and prevents sudden panic mid-tow.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Once you secure a contact carry 30 feet from shore, you should save breath by swimming silently to shallow water.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to your towing drag if you begin an armpit tow before coaching the tired swimmer to level their hips?
Under what condition does a rescuer switch from a simple armpit tow to a firmer cross-chest carry during a 30-foot swim?
Which visual check confirms the subject's mouth and nose remain clear of wash while you swim sidestroke in a cross-chest carry?
Why is it dangerous to clamp your forearm across the victim's throat instead of crossing snugly over the collarbone and chest?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Submerging immediately makes the victim release their hold so they can reach upward toward the surface for air.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Fighting to stay at the surface gives you better leverage to pry loose a victim's arms from a front head hold.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pulling straight back locks against four fingers, whereas rotating and driving toward the thumb opens the weakest gap.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Yanking your arm straight back toward your chest is the fastest way to break a panicked swimmer's grip on your wrist.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Tucking your chin to protect your windpipe, submerging, and pushing up on their elbows lets you spin safely behind them.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Escaping a rear headlock requires striking the victim with your elbows to force them to let go of your neck.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Once free, you push back into a reverse-and-ready position to reassess the subject and continue the rescue safely.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: After breaking a wrist grasp at the surface, you should immediately dive deep and swim away toward the shore.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a panicked victim's grip around your neck as soon as you tuck your chin and take both of you underwater?
Which anatomical weak point in the subject's hand allows you to break a wrist grasp cleanly without winning a strength contest?
Where should a Scout position the chin and hands when twisting out of a rear headlock and moving behind the subject?
Why is it dangerous to surface directly in front of the victim after breaking free from a front head-and-shoulder hold?

extra_misconceptions.fact: An exhausted swimmer may still be conscious and panic when touched, so always shout and splash water before making contact.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A swimmer floating face-down and motionless at the surface is always completely unconscious and safe to grab immediately.

extra_misconceptions.fact: You must swim with your head up using a modified crawl or breaststroke so you never lose sight of a sinking victim.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Putting your head down for a racing freestyle sprint is the best way to cover 30 feet to an unconscious victim.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Moving behind the victim to support the head and chin while rotating them faceup keeps the airway clear of the surface.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rolling a face-down unconscious subject over in deep water requires pushing one shoulder down toward the bottom.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A two-person armpit-and-knee lift or a supported beach drag removes the victim faster without risking a drop or back injury.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A single rescuer should always carry an unconscious adult out of shallow water using a fireman's shoulder lift.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to grab a motionless floating swimmer without first speaking loudly and splashing water at their face?
Which entry technique keeps your eyes locked on a floating victim 30 feet out so you do not lose their spot in dark water?
What physical cue during a 30-foot tow confirms an unconscious subject's airway is staying above the waterline?
Where should a Scout position the hands when assisting a partner to lift and drag an unresponsive victim onto the beach?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Hyperventilating blows off carbon dioxide that triggers your urge to breathe, causing sudden underwater blackout without warning.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Taking five or six rapid, deep breaths before a surface dive adds extra oxygen to your blood for a longer search.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Murky water hides stumps, rocks, and weeds, making a feetfirst surface dive mandatory whenever bottom visibility is poor.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Headfirst pike surface dives are safe in any lake as long as the water is at least eight to ten feet deep.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Wind and surface currents drift bubbles away quickly, so you must align stationary objects on the shore to mark the spot.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Floating bubbles and surface rings mark the exact spot where a submerged swimmer rests on the bottom several seconds later.

extra_misconceptions.fact: You press both palms downward to lift your torso out of the water, letting your body weight sink you straight down.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: During a feetfirst surface dive, kicking downward with a flutter kick is the way to drop below the surface.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to your search accuracy if you only watch the water ripples instead of sighting two fixed landmarks on shore?
Under what condition does a rescuer choose a feetfirst surface dive over a faster headfirst pike dive in 10 feet of water?
Which physical sensation in your ears tells you to pinch your nose and equalize pressure before reaching 10 feet of depth?
Why is it dangerous to hyperventilate rapidly at the surface before making repeated 10-foot dives for a submerged subject?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Vertebrae can be fractured or unstable before the spinal cord is severed, so any head-impact dive requires full immobilization.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A swimmer who can still wiggle their fingers and toes after hitting bottom in a shallow dive does not have a spinal injury.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The head-splint technique clamps the victim's own upper arms firmly against their ears to stabilize the head without neck torque.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Turning a facedown spinal victim in chest-deep water is done by gripping their chin and forehead with your hands.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Warm water supports the body evenly, so a breathing spinal subject stays supported in shallow water until a backboard arrives.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rescuers should immediately drag a breathing spinal victim onto dry land so paramedics can reach them faster.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Jumping creates waves that jostle the victim's damaged neck, so you must use a slow slide-in entry to keep the water calm.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Using a compact jump entry near a suspected spinal victim in waist-deep water saves critical rescue time.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to cervical spine alignment if you rotate a facedown victim on the spot without gliding them forward first?
Where should a Scout position the victim's upper arms during a head-splint turn to lock the neck and torso together?
Which physical indicator or mechanism of injury requires you to manage a conscious swimmer as a suspected spinal case?
Why is it dangerous to lift a breathing spinal injury victim onto the pool deck without a backboard and trained help?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Drowning arrest is caused by severe oxygen depletion, so delivering effective rescue breaths is essential to survival.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hands-only CPR without rescue breaths is just as effective for drowning victims as it is for sudden cardiac arrest on land.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Abdominal thrusts delay ventilations and force stomach contents into the airway, so begin rescue breaths and CPR immediately.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rescuers must press on a drowning victim's stomach to push water out of the lungs before starting rescue breathing.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Irregular agonal gasps do not move air into the lungs and are a sign of cardiac arrest requiring immediate resuscitation.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Occasional snorting or reflex gasping from an unconscious swimmer means they are breathing well enough to skip CPR.

extra_misconceptions.fact: As long as the victim is out of standing puddles and the chest skin is wiped dry before pad placement, an AED is safe to use.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: An automated external defibrillator cannot be used on a drowning victim who was just pulled onto a damp pool deck.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to skip rescue breaths and use hands-only compressions on an unresponsive victim pulled from the water?
Which physical indicator distinguishes ineffective agonal gasping from normal breathing during your 10-second assessment?
What compression depth and rate confirm your chest compressions are circulating oxygenated blood effectively on an adult?
What happens to the electrical current from an AED if you apply pads to a dripping-wet chest without wiping it dry first?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Hyperventilation purges carbon dioxide without adding oxygen, suppressing the breathing reflex until blackout occurs underwater.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hyperventilating before diving underwater stores extra oxygen in the lungs so a swimmer can safely hold their breath longer.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Vigorous rubbing and rapid extremity heating drive cold blood to the heart, triggering dangerous cardiac arrhythmias and shock.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing a hypothermic swimmer's arms and legs vigorously or placing them in a hot shower is the fastest way to restore warmth.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Fresh water changes osmotic pressure and causes undischarged nematocysts to fire more venom; rinse with vinegar or saltwater.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rinsing a saltwater jellyfish sting with fresh drinking water immediately neutralizes the remaining tentacles on the skin.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Exertion in water still causes heavy sweat loss, and water surfaces reflect ultraviolet rays that intensify sunburn exposure.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Swimmers immersed in cool lake or ocean water do not sweat or lose body fluids fast enough to develop dehydration or sunburn.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to purposefully hyperventilate before attempting an underwater distance swim?
Which physical indicator distinguishes life-threatening heatstroke from heat exhaustion on an exposed boat deck?
What timing and vital-sign details belong in a waterfront medical log when rewarming a hypothermic swimmer?
Where should a swimmer position their body in deep water to safely stretch out a sudden gastrocnemius calf cramp?
